findings.topic: Clerical hopes and cumulative losses
findings.source_grounded_note: Priests’ June alliance seeks peace and relief, not clear surrender of order/veto. Lost tithes, fees, benefices, dues, property, and worship monopoly turn early goodwill into insecurity; salary promises vary in value and timing.

findings.topic: Dissolution of religious houses and Catholic-state demand
findings.source_grounded_note: Exemptions protect charitable/educational houses, while contemplatives and new vows are rejected as useless. Joseph II and earlier French closures provide precedents; Dom Gerle’s failed motion exposes fear about Catholic standing.

findings.topic: Montauban and Nîmes: confessional shifts in power
findings.source_grounded_note: Protestant wealth, electoral organization, and militias face Catholic municipal majorities. Montauban’s anti-inventory riot and Nîmes’s deadly bagarre differ in sequence/outcome; Gard administration identifies Revolution with Protestant ascendancy for local Catholics.

findings.topic: Avignon, Comtat, and papal relations
findings.source_grounded_note: Local annexationism, rival councils, violence, and civil war precede French acceptance. Popular-will claims do not prove Comtat consensus; territory also becomes imagined leverage over Pius VI in ecclesiastical negotiation.

findings.topic: Ecclesiastical committee and unilateral religious reconstruction
findings.source_grounded_note: Lay expansion of the committee overcomes clerical hesitation. Many reformers are sincere Catholics seeking early-church discipline; denial of papal administrative competence and rejection of a national council leave no alternative ecclesiastical authority to papal dissent.

findings.topic: Civil Constitution: rationalization versus appointment
findings.source_grounded_note: Departmental dioceses, fewer parishes, residence, experience requirements, salaries, and abolition of non-pastoral benefices differ from disputed lay election and exclusion of papal confirmation. Useful administrative reform does not resolve canonical authority.

findings.topic: Richerism and limits of elective church governance
findings.source_grounded_note: Priestly synods inspired by Edmond Richer are not equivalent to election by active citizens who may be non-Catholic or atheist. Preserve clerical versus lay participation.

findings.topic: Papal silence, royal sanction, and uncertainty
findings.source_grounded_note: Pius’s private objection precedes adoption, yet bishops initially press Rome to accommodate reform and misread royal promulgation as evidence of settlement. Delay and silence leave priests uncertain while local implementation accelerates.

findings.topic: Jacobin clubs and political apprenticeship
findings.source_grounded_note: Breton/Revolution Club develops into Friends of the Constitution; provincial affiliation, correspondence, festivals, newspapers, and pressure on officials extend elite associative habits into politics. Religious contests are a principal catalyst, not the only one.

findings.topic: Jalès and Catholic counter-revolutionary organization
findings.source_grounded_note: A patriotic Guard federation is captured by defeated Nîmes Catholic leaders, then leaves a committee connecting local grievances to Artois’s plans. Distinguish stages of the gathering from labeling all federation participants originally counter-revolutionary.

findings.topic: Exposition of Principles and imposed clerical oath
findings.source_grounded_note: Bishops ask for ecclesiastical authorization rather than armed rebellion. Enforcement, denied confirmations, dismissals, and withheld salaries precede the oath as a compulsory public choice with replacement for refusal.

findings.topic: Oath as decisive political division
findings.source_grounded_note: The Assembly expects few refusers but confronts roughly half the clergy. The source treats compulsory choice as its gravest mistake and as paradoxically legitimizing refusal. Geographic variation and parishioner pressure qualify simple financial or hierarchical explanations.

findings.topic: Geography and social bases of oath-taking
findings.source_grounded_note: Paris/plains, Pyrenees, Provence/Dauphiné contrast with Flanders, Alsace, Languedoc, and western refusal. Congruiste resentment and western locally rooted priests matter, but community attitudes connect the oath to wider judgments of the Revolution.

findings.topic: Constitutional Church, careers, and staffing shortfall
findings.source_grounded_note: Talleyrand ensures episcopal succession; former monks/canons seek new benefices and income. Refusal leaves too many vacancies, forcing retention of nonjurors pending replacements; papal texts trigger some sworn clergy to retract.

findings.topic: Papal publication and breach with Rome
findings.source_grounded_note: March/April papal texts become public in May and are treated as condemnation despite stopping short of an explicit formula. Anti-papal protest and suppression of refractory worship clash with declared religious rights; nuncio departs.

findings.topic: Counter-revolution’s popular base and émigré limits
findings.source_grounded_note: Religious division supplies support previously missing beyond sectarian districts. Mirabeau secretly seeks a stronger monarchy within revolutionary gains; Artois/Calonne aim at reversal. Rhône/Lyons and second Jalès plots fail, and émigré headquarters move from Turin to Koblenz.

findings.topic: Army mutiny and Bouillé
findings.source_grounded_note: Rank resentment of aristocratic officers, Guard influence, and local Jacobin support culminate at Nancy. Bouillé’s bloody suppression temporarily restores discipline and makes him a potential royal rescuer.

findings.topic: Religious conscience and royal escape preparations
findings.source_grounded_note: King’s doubts grow through oath refusals and Rome’s silence; aunts’ departure, Day of Daggers, and blocked Saint-Cloud excursion intensify confinement. No evidence makes Saint-Cloud an existing escape plan; its prevention helps cause later flight.

findings.topic: Parisian activism and social-economic pressure
findings.source_grounded_note: Women, Cordeliers, popular societies, and radical press attack clerical/royal retreat; Lafayette pleases neither radicals nor royalists. Emigration and church closures cut employment, charity workshops respond, and depreciating assignats raise prices.

findings.topic: Guild abolition, wage organizing, and Le Chapelier Law
findings.source_grounded_note: End of guild/employer corporations encourages labour combinations and minimum-wage/strike demands. Municipal opposition culminates in prohibiting worker organization, collective action, and recognition by authorities.

findings.topic: Moderation of early radicals and political exclusion
findings.source_grounded_note: Le Chapelier and the Barnave–Duport–Lameth triumvirate seek consolidation; Monarchical Club fails. Robespierre’s motions bar executive posts and reelection of Constituent deputies, aided by right-wing tactical support.

findings.topic: Robespierre’s emerging prominence and uncertain republicanism
findings.source_grounded_note: British observers anticipate influence while deputies dismiss him; the author doubts that he is already republican and records his denial. Colonial rights and election as public prosecutor strengthen his position.

findings.topic: Colonial rights, slavery, and free people of colour
findings.source_grounded_note: Barnave’s committee protects slavery; Saint-Domingue whites resist free-coloured political claims. Robespierre opposes slavery and supports rights independent of colour. Distinguish enslaved people, free coloureds, and white colonists rather than treating all colonial rights as identical.

findings.topic: Varennes: organization, interception, and unresolved intention
findings.source_grounded_note: Fersen coordinates flight toward Montmédy with Bouillé’s escorts; delays, suspicious troop movements, recognition at Sainte-Ménehould, and Drouet’s intervention lead to Varennes capture. Negotiating from safety versus foreign-backed return remains uncertain.

findings.topic: Royal manifesto and Assembly’s kidnapping fiction
findings.source_grounded_note: The king rejects confinement, property violations, weak executive, clubs, and religious change. Assembly preserves monarchy despite functioning without him, suspends him, and blames Bouillé, fearing republican pressure and constitutional reconstruction.

findings.topic: Republican mobilization and Jacobin split
findings.source_grounded_note: Cordeliers demand deposition/referendum; affiliated clubs divide and mostly stop short of explicit republicanism. Social Circle/Bouche de fer petition drives Feuillant secession; Robespierre withdraws Jacobin support too late.

findings.topic: Champ de Mars massacre and repression
findings.source_grounded_note: Two lynchings prompt martial law; Guard fire follows stones/shots into a largely unarmed crowd. Killings, arrests, press closures, and flight/going into hiding temporarily break radical organization and enable final constitutional work.

findings.topic: Final constitutional revision and constrained politics
findings.source_grounded_note: Barnave’s royal conciliation excludes Civil Constitution from entrenched constitutional law and rejects harsher refractory exclusion. Silver-mark removal is offset by richer elector qualifications; press restrictions pass while broader monarchien proposals fail.

findings.topic: Émigré law, amnesty, and army officer exodus
findings.source_grounded_note: Return deadlines/triple taxation and lists precede amnesty; Varennes, loyalty oaths, and mutinies drive massive officer departure. Some leave under pressure rather than uncomplicated voluntary political rejection.

findings.topic: Padua, Pillnitz, and perception versus intent
findings.source_grounded_note: Leopold seeks concerted monarchical action, but limited response and Austrian demobilization make Pillnitz chiefly a conditional honour gesture. Émigré publication and war rumours turn it into provocation in France.

findings.topic: Failure of Feuillant consensus and Constituent legacy
findings.source_grounded_note: Most provincial Jacobins stay affiliated; nobles withhold support and king’s sincerity is doubted. Constitution, amnesty, annexation, and Assembly’s end coexist with schism and republican polarization. The source credits durable institutional achievement while locating seeds of future extremes in these unresolved divisions.

uncertainties.note: Dom Gerle’s motion is dated 12 April on page 137 and 13 April on page 142. Preserve the conflict rather than silently choosing a date.
Early republicanism of Robespierre is doubted by the author despite contemporary British claims; do not transform the observers’ inference into fact.
No evidence establishes Saint-Cloud as an escape plan; the ultimate purpose of the later flight is also left unresolved.

bindings.source_page_basis: one-based document pages and identical printed numeric labels

artifact_role: Source-first omission/readership notes only; not a canonical benchmark, typed editorial review, approval, or freeze.
